sm: The episode opens with the Mountain Valley pipeline, a roughly three hundred mile natural gas line approved in 2017. It was projected to cost three and a half billion dollars and finish in 2018, but it was completed in June 2024, more than five years late and at nine point six billion dollars. The narrator blames permitting, meaning the reviews, agencies, lawsuits and paperwork, and says the Senate just passed a bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for energy and data infrastructure. Host Jack Spencer then interviews Senator Alan Armstrong, a former Williams Companies chairman with a background in highways, bridges and pipelines. Armstrong says permits are now granted and later voided by courts, and that this hurts consumers and the poor, citing the Vogtle nuclear overrun.

Armstrong recalls Williams spending four hundred million dollars on a project with a federal permit before New York blocked it, and says that risk raises returns that end up in utility bills. He explains the bill's main changes. The window to sue shrinks from six years to one hundred fifty days, and claims must have been raised during the permitting process. Under laws like the Clean Water Act, agencies must show they asked for the least burdensome solution. Linear projects that expand their right of way by less than twenty percent would skip a major NEPA review. He says the bill does not lower environmental standards, and cites a Washington sewer line stuck in review for seven and a half years that ruptured and spilled two hundred fifty million gallons of sewage into the Potomac.

The two discuss claims that the bill guts environmental rules. Armstrong says what it guts is the cottage industry of sue and settle, which Spencer defines as groups suing the government and settling in ways that favor their position. On the transmission provisions, Armstrong says the Federal Power Act already gives FERC authority and eminent domain, and the bill codifies it while letting states act first. He acknowledges the real argument is how costs are allocated. He argues the country must be able to build interstate projects, noting that in Dubai permitting barely translated as a concept. He adds that he grew up in a ranching family and understands landowner concerns.

Spencer calls the bipartisan bill imperfect but good overall, and worries a future FERC could use public interest findings against fossil fuels. Armstrong replies that the bill does not pick winners and losers, so cheaper sources of any kind can win. He says the difference from the earlier Manchin and Barrasso effort is that renewables, hydropower, geothermal, mining and pipeline industries all stayed united. He credits Senators Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich, and staff on the National Energy Dominance Council. Spencer then praises a manager's amendment letting uranium enrichment facilities start construction before getting an operating permit, as long as safety standards are met and no operation begins without the permit.

Spencer says the uranium provision could cut years off building capacity and help end reliance on Russian uranium. Armstrong adds that the bill includes a mining measure from Senators Risch and Cortez Masto, and that geothermal gained the most, without subsidies. He urges House members to take the bill as a whole, since another chance is unlikely for a couple of years. On affordability, he says blocked pipelines raise rates, and notes New England pays heavily for fuel oil while gas costs far less. He says Senate Democrats are trying poison pill amendments, chiefly one from Ron Wyden barring federal data centers on public lands. Armstrong closes optimistically, saying passage would be a major vote of confidence for the country.
